At the Last Supper Jesus Washes the Disciples' Feet--The Discourse Arising Thereupon.</title> <div sID="gen29391" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15284"/><hi type="bold">1. when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father--</hi>On these beautiful euphemisms, see on <reference osisRef="Luke.9.31">Lu 9:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.9.51">Lu 9:51</reference>.<div eID="gen29391" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29392" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end--</hi>The meaning is, that on the very edge of His last sufferings, when it might have been supposed that He would be absorbed in His own awful prospects, He was so far from forgetting "His own," who were to be left struggling "in the world" after He had "departed out of it to the Father" (<reference osisRef="John.17.11">Joh 17:11</reference>), that in His care for them He seemed scarce to think of Himself save in connection with them: "Herein is love," not only "enduring to the end," but most affectingly manifested when, judging by a human standard, least to be expected. <div eID="gen29392" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 13 Joh 13:1-20 . At the Last Supper Jesus Washes the Disciples' Feet--The Discourse Arising Thereupon. 1. when Jesus knew that his hour was come that he should depart out of this world unto the Father-- On these beautiful euphemisms, see on Lu 9:31 ; Lu 9:51 . having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end-- The meaning is, that on the very edge of His last sufferings, when it might have been supposed that He would be absorbed in His own awful prospects, He was so far from forgetting "His own," who were to be left struggling "in the world" after He had "departed out of it to the Father" ( Joh 17:11 ), that in His care for them He seemed scarce to think of Himself save in connection with them: "Herein is love," not only "enduring to the end," but most affectingly manifested when, judging by a human standard, least to be expected.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15289"/><div sID="gen29400" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15289"/><hi type="bold">6-11. Peter saith ... Lord, dost thou wash my feet?--</hi>Our language cannot bring out the intensely vivid contrast between the "Thou" and the "my," which, by bringing them together, the original expresses, for it is not good English to say, "Lord, Thou my feet dost wash?" But every word of this question is emphatic. Thus far, and in the question itself, there was nothing but the most profound and beautiful astonishment at a condescension to him quite incomprehensible. Accordingly, though there can be no doubt that already Peter's heart rebelled against it as a thing not to be tolerated, Jesus ministers no rebuke as yet, but only bids him wait a little, and he should understand it all. <div eID="gen29400" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15301"/><title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="John.13.21-John.13.30">Joh 13:21-30</reference>. The Traitor Indicated--He Leaves the Supper Room.</title> <div sID="gen29429" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15301"/><hi type="bold">21. When Jesus had thus said, he was troubled in spirit, and testified, and said, Verily, verily, I say unto you, One of you shall betray me--</hi>The announcement of <reference osisRef="John.13.18">Joh 13:18</reference> seems not to have been plain enough to be quite apprehended, save by the traitor himself. He will therefore speak it out in terms not to be misunderstood. But how much it cost Him to do this, appears from the "trouble" that came over His "spirit"--visible emotion, no doubt--before He got it uttered. What wounded susceptibility does this disclose, and what exquisite delicacy in His social intercourse with the Twelve, to whom He cannot, without an effort, break the subject! <div eID="gen29429" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15302"/><div sID="gen29430" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15302"/><hi type="bold">22. the disciples looked one on another, doubting of whom he spake--</hi>Further intensely interesting particulars are given in the other Gospels: (1) "They were exceeding sorrowful" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.22">Mt 26:22</reference>). (2) "They began to inquire among themselves which of them it was that should do this thing" (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.23">Lu 22:23</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.3">3</reference>) "They began to say unto Him one by one, Is it I, and another, Is it I?" (<reference osisRef="Mark.14.19">Mr 14:19</reference>). Generous, simple hearts! They abhorred the thought, but, instead of putting it on others, each was only anxious to purge himself and know if he could be the wretch. Their putting it at once to Jesus Himself, as knowing doubtless who was to do it, was the best, as it certainly was the most spontaneous and artless evidence of their innocence. (4) Jesus, apparently while this questioning was going on, added, "The Son of man goeth as it is written of Him, but woe unto that man by whom the Son of man is betrayed! It had been good for that man if he had not been born" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.24">Mt 26:24</reference>). (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.5">5</reference>) "Judas," last of all, "answered and said, Lord, is it I?" evidently feeling that when all were saying this, if he held his peace, that of itself would draw suspicion upon him. To prevent this the question is wrung out of him, but perhaps, amidst the stir and excitement at the table, in a half-suppressed tone as we are inclined to think the answer also was--"Thou hast said" (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.25">Mt 26:25</reference>), or possibly by little more than a sign; for from <reference osisRef="John.13.28">Joh 13:28</reference> it is evident that till the moment when he went out, he was not openly discovered. <div eID="gen29430" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv15306"/><div sID="gen29438" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv15306"/><hi type="bold">27-30. after the sop Satan entered into him--</hi>Very solemn are these brief hints of the successive steps by which Judas reached the climax of his guilt. "The devil had already put it into his heart to betray his Lord." Yet who can tell what struggles he went through ere he brought himself to carry that suggestion into effect? Even after this, however, his compunctions were not at an end. With the thirty pieces of silver already in his possession, he seems still to have quailed--and can we wonder? When Jesus stooped to wash his feet, it may be the last struggle was reaching its crisis. But that word of the Psalm, about "one that ate of his bread who would lift up his heel against Him" (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.9">Psa 41:9</reference>) probably all but turned the dread scale, and the still more explicit announcement, that one of those sitting with Him at the table should betray Him, would beget the thought, "I am detected; it is now too late to draw back." At that moment the sop is given; offer of friendship is once more made--and how affectingly! But already "Satan has entered into him," and though the Saviour's act might seem enough to recall him even yet, hell is now in his bosom, and he says within himself, "The die is cast; now let me go through with it"; fear, begone!" (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.12.43">Mt 12:43</reference>).<div eID="gen29438" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29439" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Then said Jesus unto him, That thou doest, do quickly--</hi>that is, Why linger here? Thy presence is a restraint, and thy work stands still; thou hast the wages of iniquity, go work for it! <div eID="gen29439" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 27-30. after the sop Satan entered into him-- Very solemn are these brief hints of the successive steps by which Judas reached the climax of his guilt. When Jesus stooped to wash his feet, it may be the last struggle was reaching its crisis. But that word of the Psalm, about "one that ate of his bread who would lift up his heel against Him" ( Psa 41:9 ) probably all but turned the dread scale, and the still more explicit announcement, that one of those sitting with Him at the table should betray Him, would beget the thought, "I am detected; it is now too late to draw back." But already "Satan has entered into him," and though the Saviour's act might seem enough to recall him even yet, hell is now in his bosom, and he says within himself, "The die is cast; now let me go through with it"; fear, begone!" (See on Mt 12:43 ). Then said Jesus unto him, That thou doest, do quickly-- that is, Why linger here? Thy presence is a restraint, and thy work stands still; thou hast the wages of iniquity, go work for it!

entries.content_plain: 32. If God be glorified in him, God shall also-- in return and reward of this highest of all services ever rendered to Him, or capable of being rendered. glorify him in himself, and ... straightway glorify him-- referring now to the Resurrection and Exaltation of Christ after this service was over, including all the honor and glory then put upon Him, and that will for ever encircle Him as Head of the new creation.

entries.content_plain: 33-35. Little children-- From the height of His own glory He now descends, with sweet pity, to His "little children," all now His own. This term of endearment, nowhere else used in the Gospels, and once only employed by Paul ( Ga 4:19 ), is appropriated by the beloved disciple himself, who no fewer than seven times employs it in his first Epistle. Ye shall seek me-- feel the want of Me. as I said to the Jews-- ( Joh 7:34 ; 8:21 ). But oh in what a different sense!

entries.content_plain: 36-38. Peter said-- seeing plainly in these directions how to behave themselves, that He was indeed going from them. Lord, whither guest thou?-- having hardly a glimmer of the real truth. Jesus answered, ... thou canst not follow me now, but thou shalt follow me afterwards-- How different from what He said to the Jews: "Whither I go ye cannot come" ( Joh 8:21 ).
